newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone talks hit hurdle over rebel leader.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone talks hit hurdle over rebel leader.

text.p: Talks to end the political crisis in Sierra Leone hit a hurdle on Tuesday over the detention in Nigeria of rebel leader Foday Sankoh, conference sources said.
West African foreign ministers and envoys of the ruling junta in Freetown opened talks earlier in Ivory Coast on restoring civilian rule after a May 25 coup in Sierra Leone.
But the talks broke off briefly after about half an hour with the Freetown delegation insisting that Sankoh, whose rebels rallied to the coup, join them at the meeting, one source said.
Talks were reconvening later in the day, delegates said.
"It's clear that they want Sankoh to be part of the negotiations," one conference source told reporters.
Sankoh's Revolutionray United Front (RUF) waged a five-year bush war in Sierra Leone from 1991 before signing an accord in November 1996 with then civilian president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah.
Junior officers toppled Kabbah two months ago, accusing him of violating the accord with Sankoh. RUF guerrillas rallied to the coup and entered the capital in their thousands.
Sankoh, who was in Nigeria at the time, was detained in prison after he ordered his men to join the coup soldiers.
The coup has been condemned worldwide, with the international community demanding the restoration of Kabbah.

Nigerian troops leading a regional military force, ECOMOG, bombarded Freetown on June 2 trying to reverse the coup. The poorly coordinated attack failed and Nigeria has since joined regional efforts to negotiate the departure of the junta.

The military junta agreed in principle at a first round of talks in Abidjan on July 18 to restore civilian rule. Its spokesmen said they expected their gesture would lead to the lifting of a crippling economic embargo imposed by the Economic Community of Wedst African States (ECOWAS).
But on the eve of the latest talks, ECOMOG commanders ruled out an end to the embargo, warning ships and aircraft to keep clear of the country.
Fuel and food are running short in Freetown, which had already faced severe hardship after an orgy of looting that followed the coup. Shops and banks remain closed.
Conference sources said they had expected negotiations to be difficult after the military junta decided to change nearly all the members of its previous delegation.
All but about three of the 17 members of Tuesday's delegation were new.
Nigerian Foreign Minister Tom Ikimi, whose country holds the ECOWAS presidency, opened Tuesday's talks saying they were expected to deal only with the restoration of democratic rule.
The ECOWAS committee comprises foreign ministers from regional giant Nigeria, Ghana, Guinea and host Ivory Coast.
"We do not expect that the meeting will be taking too much of our time," Ikimi said. "We intend to build on progress made at the last meeting."

Diplomats said earlier that the talks had been put back from last Friday to allow the Freetown junta more time to meet the committee's demand for the restoration of Kabbah, who fled to exile in Guinea.
